#2769. Wolves 104, Grizzlies 95: Defense Downs the Bear

Basketball is a funny thing. One night, the world is obsessed with your offense-capping defensive stalwart and the next you're holding the number one offense in all of basketball to 95 points while that aforementioned rim protector has an incredible game (and still missed some layups).

In a game in which they looked dominant throughout, the Minnesota Timberwolves taught the Memphis Grizzlies that there is joy in being a young, upstart team, but it is still incredibly hard to face off with a capable team on a random Saturday with some of your best players absent.

No, luckily, the Wolves have seemingly learned this lesson.

Minnesota's nine-point margin is significantly smaller than it likely should be after the Grizzlies outscored them by 12 in the fourth quarter. Don't be fooled, this was functionally a wire to wire victory.

The Wolves employed a bit of a platoon plan on offense tonight, spreading usage to each of the starters and allowing Jonathan Kuminga, Jaden McDaniels, and Ayo Dosunmu to all turn in impressive point totals. This Wolves team just keeps showing up and playing well in a way that could not be further from what Wolves fans are used to. Memphis leaned on Cedric Coward and Most Improved Player frontrunner Ty Jerome, but struggled to do much of anything until a garbage time run.

This was a game that put the floor of the Wolves on display more than its ceiling. This was a close win against an admittedly great team with clear weaknesses. If we're going to start there, with the two-in-one ceiling capper and floor raiser, there's only one man to talk about.

Look, the discourse surrounding Rudy Gobert does make sense. He may be the single greatest floor-raising defensive presence since Tim Duncan or Hakeem Olajuwon, but he also makes those two look like Moses combined with prime Escalade on offense.

(And yes, folks, going from being a bad catcher of the basketball to a stone-handed anomaly who is putting up 40ish% on layups is, in fact, a major regression).

Tonight was one of those nights where everything looked decent for Gobert, even if he only scored seven points. Considering the state of the timeline over the past few days – if you are lobbying for Myles Turner, you live in a 2K fanfiction – it was nice to have a reminder of what a *good* Gobert game can look like.

Anytime Minnesota has a great defensive game, everyone will place the flowers at Gobert's feet. This is, after all, exactly what he was supposed to do here. However, the hand-wave of "Gobert was great" doesn't give him his full deserved credit. Memphis did not look at the rim all game. That meant that by the time they got hot, they were in two deep of a hole to get out of.

The man may be an absolute deadbeat, have the health/food knowledge of a yule log (maybe one that's worm-eaten too), but he is an absurdly game-altering talent.

It may be impossible to replace him, and no one seems willing to give up anything of value for him. At that point, it seems the future holds a lot of floor-raising. After tonight, that sounds pretty perfect.

Five different players hit double digits for Minnesota tonight. Jaden McDaniels (25 points on 11/17 from the field), Ayo Dosunmu (19 points), Jonathan Kuminga (16 points on 6/9 shooting), LaMelo Ball (on 50% from the field after a bad stretch), and TJ Shannon Jr. each scored over 10 points, and together they provided all but 17 points in this game.

The headliner is a hyper-efficient Jaden McDaniels game, but it feels like he is destined to never truly empty the clip, instead opting to be a capable third option no matter who he is sharing the court with. Some days, he's the number three guy to Anthony Edwards and LaMelo Ball; other days, he's letting Greg Monroe initiate the offense while on a 10-day. Tonight, however, he deferred to Kuminga and Ayo as the two turned defense into offense.

However, the real storyline is TJ Shannon, who continues to rise up the depth chart (much to my personal surprise) as another change-of-pace option in attacking the rim. His 15 points in 26 minutes comes after he looked to have found some confidence and comfort in his last few games.

There was a tweet from a few weeks ago that sticks with me about this team. It said the Wolves have on of the best 1-9s in the league, but have the most garbage 10- 15s as well.

Depth is so hard to really pull off, but the Wolves have the right kind of options. Instead of playing around waiting for a loophole, Minnesota just straight up outperformed and out delivered what the Grizzlies could do off the bench.

The Wolves will face off against Julius Randle and the Brooklyn Nets Monday evening, 6:30pm CT on Peacock, as the two former allies will fight over who deserves their low ppg elbow touches. Considering all of this is about raising the floor, the 3-12 Nets probably wish they pursued Gobert instead of Randle.

#2768. Cathie Wood’s Ark Invest was a big buyer of Anthropic as she tells CNBC she’s ‘quite optimistic’

Cathie Wood was a major buyer of Anthropic following its debut Thursday on the Nasdaq, adding shares in all her major funds.

Wood's firm, which already owned private shares of the artificial intelligence company in its Ark Venture Fund leading up to the initial public offering, bought $90.8 million worth of Anthropic in six funds, according to a trade notification from the firm.

"We've owned Anthropic since early '23," Wood told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Friday. "It's our best performing equity by far in ARKVX, our venture fund. ... Our confidence has grown with time as it really took over the enterprise" AI business.

Anthropic shares jumped 17% in their first day, but closed well off the highs of the session and were headed for sizable losses Friday. The Nasdaq, which was expected to get a boost from a major IPO reviving enthusiasm about the technology trade, fell by 2% on Thursday.

"We're climbing a wall of worry," said Wood. "Everybody is worried about AI hype and the political situation after the election, but I think we'll look back and say, OK this is more like the '80s and '90s, climbing a wall of worry you know with bricks much like what we have today: inflation, interest rates, wars, new technologies and so forth so quite optimistic here."

The Anthropic stakes are relatively small across the funds, but Wood typically will buy shares in companies she likes steadily during long stretches. Wood said she is "averaging down" with her purchases of Anthropic.

In her $6.1 billion Ark Innovation ETF, Anthropic is a 0.3% stake. The biggest holdings in that fund are Tesla and SpaceX, representing more than 21% of the fund together.

Ark Innovation, which retail investors piled into during the pandemic as it gained about 150% in 2020, tumbled the subsequent next two years, losing 67% in 2022 alone. Wood's following was dented after the big losses.

The fund had a comeback stretch as the bull market revved back up from 2023 to 2025, but has fallen on hard times again this year, down more than 10% in 2026. The S&P 500 is up 4.8% this year.

Wood dismissed comparisons of today's environment to the dot-com bubble.

"Back then if an Anthropic had gone public, it probably would have gone up threefold the first day," she said. "That's how crazy things were."

#2765. Mikal Bridges is finding his groove at the right time

Remember when we all said we wouldn't care about the regular season that much after the championship? That lasted long…

As the Knicks stumbled out to a 0-3 start that didn't seem to stabilize that much until this four-game winning streak that's brought them to 10-6 ahead of tonight's game against Indiana, fans didn't seem to have the patience they promised after this same group showed they can be trusted to step up when it counts.

At the center of that impatience was Mikal Bridges, who, despite putting up a second straight awesome playoff run and fully validating the trade by helping hoist a Larry O'Brien Trophy, was the common target early on as he struggled to find his groove.

Through 11 games, he was averaging just 5.9 points a game on a rough 32.9% from the field and 26.5% from deep. He'd be benched early in games where he didn't have it for Landry Shamet, he looked even more apprehensive than usual, and his defense wasn't as impactful as usual.

We've seen bad stretches from Bridges plenty over the last two years, but this was just maddening. The ring was supposed to free him; it was supposed to allow him to tap into the best of his game for extended stretches. The weight was off his shoulders.

Instead, it just seemed to get heavier? At times, it looked like the yips, basketball edition.

But this is why you exercise patience. These guys are champions; they know how to manage the highs and lows. When they look lost, they'll figure it out.

Body language is a big deal sometimes. You started to see him break out of his shell against the Pacers, where he looked for his shot early and often. When his jumper failed him, he got to the rim. He wasn't getting to the line, but he was attacking gaps and making good reads. The activity was back defensively.

Suddenly, he was everywhere defensively. A switch seemed to flip, and it looked like he was back in that Boston series. Needing a big late comeback, he set the tone defensively. Everything he did was purposeful, as he was a +15 in the overtime victory.

The offense came back around two nights later when the Knicks really needed it. Despite being -14 in 30 minutes, he put up an efficient 17 points.

The confidence to take shots like these just wasn't there a few weeks ago. He'd miss one or two threes and just stop shooting. He'd subconsciously pass up shots that had been a part of his game for years. It's pivotal that even when the ball isn't going down that a shooter keeps shooting, and we just didn't see that.

This article comes at a great time after he called game against the Blazers on Saturday night, but I think it shows that he's got his confidence back more than anything. Watch back the tape and see if you notice anything:

First, it's the fact that he consciously looks for the ball off the inbound. A big problem with the Knicks' final-possession offense is that they have one look and no backup plan. We saw that against Indiana with KAT and we see it all the time where they just screen for Jalen Brunson to get the ball and get out of the way.

Here, Bridges goes from a screener to releasing to pop up as a backup option. Then, look at this screenshot:

There are three whole seconds left, and Toumani Camara is on a hard closeout. There is nobody near Andre Drummond underneath the basket. If Bridges immediately hits him, it's an easy dunk (or is it, with how bad his finishing has been…)

In some ways, that's the correct read. A broken inbound has left the opponent scrambling and you have an easy, game-tying bucket under the basket. Maybe if he didn't make the shot, this would be discussed more.

Regardless, the confidence of Bridges matters a whole helluva lot more than winning a regular season game. This is a guy you need in April, May, and June, not November. A 26-point blown lead sucks, blowing the first 15+-point second half lead in the regular season since April 2023 sucks, but you want him taking this shot.

Maybe he just doesn't like the Blazers. That's two game-winners against them in his three years as a Knick.

Now, if only Josh Hart can figure it out too…

#2761. Broncos, ESPN, Fox Sports and others honor longtime linebacker, analyst Tom Jackson after his death

The NFL world honored longtime Denver Broncos linebacker and ESPN analyst Tom Jackson on Sunday, days after his death.

Jackson died Friday, friend and colleague Chris Berman announced Sunday during ESPN's "Sunday NFL Countdown." He was 75.

Jackson spent 14 seasons in the league with the Broncos from 1973-1986. He earned three Pro Bowl nods and appeared in two Super Bowls with the franchise. He retired with 191 games played in his career, which was the fourth-most in Broncos history. Jackson, who played at Louisville before landing in the NFL, was inducted into Denver's Ring of Fame in 1992.

The Broncos honored Jackson ahead of their game with the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday, and played a video tribute to him on the scoreboard at Empower Field before kickoff.

Lee Corso, who coached Jackson at Louisville, called him the "best football player I ever had."

"Not only that, he was the best leader I ever had," Corso said in a statement. "My condolences to Tom's family in this difficult time."

After his playing career ended, Jackson joined ESPN in 1987 and quickly became a fixture in the network's NFL coverage. He worked there for nearly three decades until he retired in 2016, and spent nearly the entire time working alongside Berman.

"All of us are stunned. We've lost one of the best human beings ever to walk the planet," Berman said. "I was fortunate, as you know, to work side-by-side with him for 30 years on 'NFL Primetime' and 'NFL Gameday,' now 'Sunday NFL Countdown.'"

"Tom was so much more than an accomplished NFL analyst," he added. "There was nobody kinder, there was nobody more thoughtful, more loyal, more engaging than Tom Jackson."

Jackson was behind the iconic "Jacked Up!" segment each week during the NFL season, which showcased the hardest hits throughout the league. The segment was eventually phased out as concern for head trauma and serious injury grew throughout football.

ESPN brought that segment back Sunday, and ended it with a huge hit of Jackson's.

Fox Sports also honored Jackson during its coverage, and played the "NFL Primetime" music while showing halftime highlights Sunday.

NFL commissioner Roger Goodell issued a statement remembering Jackson:

"The NFL lost a wonderful man with the passing of Tom Jackson. Along with millions of fans, I will always remember him as a player and broadcaster, but also as a friend. He was an outstanding player whose toughness and leadership helped define an era of Broncos football. He brought credibility, passion and humor to everything he did, and generations of fans came to know him through his work at ESPN. Tom helped fans enjoy and better understand football, always bringing the perspective of someone who loved the game and the people who play it. More importantly, he earned the respect and friendship of players, coaches and everyone who had the privilege of knowing and working with him."

Rich Eisen, Keyshawn Johnson, Tedy Bruschi, Randy Moss, Adam Schefter, Bill Cower and plenty of others in the NFL media world all honored Jackson and spoke about him on their respective platforms.

#2758. Oklahoma State Erupts in Second Half, Routs Virginia Tech 106-80

Charleston, SC. — Oklahoma State delivered the kind of offensive performance Steve Lutz has been looking for, exploding for 65 second-half points in a 106-80 victory over Virginia Tech in the Charleston Classic.

After entering halftime tied at 41, the Cowboys shot a blistering 73.5% from the field in the final 20 minutes, turning a competitive game into a 26-point rout of the Hokies. Julius Halaifonua led Oklahoma State with 22 points on 9-of-14 shooting, while Kashie Natt delivered an outstanding all-around performance with 21 points, seven rebounds and five steals.

The Cowboys finished shooting 66.7% from the floor and 57.1% from three-point range, recording 24 assists on 42 made field goals while committing just eight turnovers. But the game was far from decided at halftime.

Virginia Tech matched Oklahoma State throughout the opening 20 minutes, with neither team able to create much separation. The Hokies led by as many as five points before the Cowboys carried a 41-39 advantage into the final minute of the half.

Jaylen Curry tied the game at 41 with a layup just before the halftime buzzer. The back-and-forth battle continued early in the second half. Ben Hammond helped Virginia Tech take a 54-51 lead with 16:31 remaining, but that would be the Hokies' final advantage.

Natt answered with a three-pointer to tie the game before Halaifonua threw down a transition dunk to put Oklahoma State ahead for good. The Cowboys gradually extended their lead before delivering the decisive stretch midway through the half. Leading 64-59 with 11:46 remaining, Oklahoma State unleashed a 13-0 run that completely changed the game.

Andrija Grbovic knocked down a three-pointer, Benjamin Ahmed converted a three-point play, and Natt added a three-pointer of his own before scoring on a fast-break layup following a steal. By the time Virginia Tech called timeout, Oklahoma State had stretched its advantage to 75-59. Natt added another steal and layup moments later to push the lead to 18.

The Cowboys never looked back. Oklahoma State continued attacking offensively, eventually building a 28-point advantage as the Hokies struggled to slow down the Cowboys' balanced scoring attack.

Halaifonua added five rebounds and three made three-pointers to his team-high 22 points. Natt was nearly perfect offensively, making eight of his nine field-goal attempts and all three of his shots from beyond the arc. He also committed zero turnovers in 26 minutes.

Luka Bogavac provided 17 points off the bench, shooting 6-of-11 from the field and 3-of-6 from three-point range. Ahmed added 11 points on a perfect 5-of-5 shooting, while Jacob Walker orchestrated the offense with nine points, nine assists and zero turnovers.

Oklahoma State received 38 points from its bench and dominated the paint with 48 points, adding 14 fast-break points and 15 points off turnovers. The Cowboys' offensive execution was particularly impressive after halftime, when they made 25 of 34 field-goal attempts, including seven of 11 three-pointers, while committing just two turnovers.

Virginia Tech was led by Hammond's 24 points, while Curry added 18 points and seven assists. The Hokies shot 43.5% from the field and 41.4% from three-point range but couldn't keep pace with Oklahoma State's second-half surge. The Cowboys also won the rebounding battle 33-27 and recorded nine steals.

For Oklahoma State, the performance represented an encouraging display of the offensive balance, ball movement and efficiency Lutz has been seeking. After a tightly contested opening half, the Cowboys turned the game into a showcase of what their offense can accomplish when multiple players contribute and the basketball moves freely.

#2754. As Anthropic shares tank, investors scramble to hedge. It could be very expensive

As Anthropic shares tumble toward their IPO price of $83, investors are looking for ways to hedge. Unfortunately, they may have to wait until Monday, when options on the AI giant are expected to list.

If Anthropic breaks its IPO price, it will represent a 27% decline from Thursday's intraday high of $113. The wild price swings offer clues on how expensive it might be to buy protection on the new tech giant once options begin trading.A 20% intraday move points to an implied volatility somewhere between 100 and 150 for Anthropic options, according to estimates from single-stock market-makers on the Cboe trading floor in Chicago.

Options traders are also looking at how SpaceX traded in the days following its offering for clues on how options might price.

Implied volatility in SpaceX started at 116, but that didn't deter options traders big and small from piling into the contracts tracking the stock, with about 1.7 million contracts traded on the first day for a total options premium of about $2.5 billion. Far out-of-the-money call contracts were some of the most popular trades as the stock soared 40% in its first three sessions.One key difference between now and then? Anthropic is trading against the backdrop of S&P 500 volatility close to 30, compared to 17.3 when SpaceX debuted. "I expect ANT options to be super active," said Tom Sosnoff, co-founder of the trading platforms ThinkOrSwim and TastyTrade. "I expect heavy options volume."One thing Anthropic and SpaceX have in common is heavy retail involvement in both IPOs, with retail brokerages receiving a 20% allocation from SpaceX and reports pointing to between a 15-20% allocation from Anthropic on Thursday. "Round one of the Anthropic IPO easily goes to the individual investor," Sosnoff added. "Retail participants bailed early at the best prices of the day while institutional investors paid up to top off their underwhelming allocations. I believe retail was aggressively reloading in the mid-90s."Further signs of retail demand will become evident when options likely begin trading on Monday. One thing to watch: the spread between out-of-the-money call and put contracts, which was heavily skewed toward calls in the case of SpaceX. "I would be careful comparing Anthropic to SpaceX," said Dennis Davitt, CIO and Co-Founder of Millbank Dartmoor Portsmouth. "From a market-structure perspective, the two are dramatically different. The availability and cost of borrowing will be different, the companies are at very different stages of maturity, and SpaceX has allowed employees to monetize portions of their holdings over time. All of those factors matter when pricing options."

Florida football is climbing The Athletic's SEC vibe rankings after securing its seventh victory of the season.

Florida's two-spot rise reflects the increasingly positive outlook surrounding the program as Sumrall approaches the end of his first regular season in Gainesville.

#2749. Jeffery Simmons picks up 3.0 more sacks, Bears beat Saints 21-13

When the Saints look back on their Week 11 loss to the Bears, they’ll likely lament several missed opportunities.

While the Bears looked rusty coming off of their Week 10 bye, they still were able to make enough plays to defeat New Orleans 21-10 on Sunday.

Chicago got out to a 16-0 lead midway through the second quarter with a 41-yard field goal and two touchdown passes from Caleb Williams, though one of them featured a missed extra point. But the Saints narrowed that lead to six points at halftime with a 1-yard pass from Tyler Shough to Alvin Kamara paired with a 56-yard field goal from Charlie Smyth.

That, however, didn’t make up for an egregiously wide right missed field goal from 47 yards out.

The Bears then extended their lead with a 35-yard field goal from Cairo Santos midway through the third quarter. And the Bears got a safety early in the fourth quarter to close out their scoring, with Montez Sweat bringing Shough down in the end zone for a sack.

The Saints got down to Chicago’s 10-yard line after a Bears fumble in the fourth quarter, but weren’t able to connect, turning it over on downs.

With no timeouts due to failed challenges, New Orleans could only manage a 51-yard field goal late in the fourth quarter before attempting an onside kick.

As most have this season, the Saints’ attempt failed.

As noted by the Fox broadcast, this was the Bears’ fifth consecutive game without trailing. It’s the franchise’s longest streak since 1959, when they had six such contests.

Williams ended the game 15-of-23 for 181 yards with two touchdowns and an interception.

The Jeffery Simmons trade continues to pay off for the Bears, as he registered 3.0 sacks on Shough. Via NFL research, Simmons is now the first Bears player to have at least 4.0 sacks in his first three games with the franchise since Khalil Mack in 2018.

Shough was 25-of-42 for 222 yards with a touchdown and a pick. Chris Olave led with 102 yards on nine catches.

Now at 8-2, the Bears will have a quick turnaround as they’ll face the Lions on the road on Thanksgiving.

The 3-7 Saints will be on the road to face the Bengals next Sunday afternoon.

#2745. The Wizards have a chance to advance in the NBA Cup

The Washington Wizards won against the Chicago Bulls last Friday. This wasn't just another regular season win. It's also their second win in NBA Cup group play, a franchise record (I'll go over why in a bit). Washington also improves to 2-1 in East Group C play.

Washington has one more game for the NBA Cup which is against the Boston Celtics on Tuesday. If they win, Washington improves to 3-1 but are mathematically eliminated from winning East Group C. It is possible that the Wizards could make the knockout stage as a wild card team if the Celtics win on Friday against the Atlanta Hawks. This would give the Celtics, Hawks and Wizards 3-1 records with the Celtics winning the group.

Now how do the Wizards claim a wildcard spot as a second place team? That's through cumulative point differential in regulation. Currently, the Wizards are third in the wildcard standings behind the Cleveland Cavaliers (+21) and the Hawks (+13) who have the same point differential as the Wizards but the Hawk hold the tiebreaker.

It will be a sign of progress if Washington can make the knockout stage of the NBA Cup. This is because Washington has finished in last place every year since 2023-24 when this tournament was introduced. In the first two years of this tournament, the Wizards finished with 0-4 group play records, while they went 1-3 last season. The Wizards also set a record two wins in group play this season, which is encouraging.

Hopefully, luck will be on their side this week when they play the Celtics on Tuesday.

(And yes, I know they host the Orlando Magic tonight).

#2744. 13 winners, 4 losers from Detroit Lions’ win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers

There was no jet lag for the Detroit Lions.

A week after their overseas tilt in Munich, Germany, the Lions returned to home turf to host the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The Buccaneers were projected to be a Minnesota Vikings-esque team—a stout defense offset by a lackluster offense. However, with Baker Mayfield healthy enough to start and Bucky Irving on a tear recently, it would not be an easy task for Detroit on either side of the football.

After a scoreless first half, the Lions woke up on offense and stayed strong on defense. The offense dropped 31 points on the NFL's best defense by Defense-adjusted Value Over Average, all while holding their own on defense. The Buccaneers finished with just 274 total yards on offense. All of a sudden, the Lions are clicking on both offense and defense:

Detroit faces a short week with Thanksgiving and the Chicago Bears on deck. Which players emerged from this game as winners or losers?

Coming off a game versus the New England Patriots in which he threw two ugly interceptions, Goff faced a tough task versus the top-ranked Buccaneers defense. In spite of the pressure, Goff delivered arguably his best game of the year.

Stat-wise, Goff has had bigger performances this season, but he was phenomenal against Tampa Bay in ways that don't show up in the numbers. The offensive line was not at its best, largely due to a large Vita Vea up the middle, yet Goff navigated the pressure swimmingly. He survived a collapsing pocket to hit Tyler Conklin for an 18-yard gain. He had a 10-yard scamper for a first down. One of Goff's best throws of the season came on his downfield shot to Jameson Williams with pressure in his grill:

Goff was not afraid to chuck it downfield, also connecting on deep shots to Sam LaPorta (47 yards) and Brock Wright (27 yards), nor did he shy away from Williams or Amon-Ra St. Brown on intermediate routes. If anything, the Lions were going away from their usual short passing attack—Jahmyr Gibbs only caught four passes for 20 yards. Goff finished the game averaging 10.0 yards per attempt, the highest average of his season thus far.

Lesser running backs would have been stonewalled by the Buccaneers defense, but Gibbs is simply too special. He is too fast and explosive to stop for an entire game. Early on, the Buccaneers admittedly had his number. However, Gibbs does the little things that make an impact over the course of a game. He ekes out any extra yard he can get. He can make defenders miss on a dime. Eventually, he can and will get his breakout plays—he is inevitable.

Gibbs turned 23 carries into 98 yards and two touchdowns, and he earned every single one of those stats. We are so lucky to witness a player like him.

On paper, the Lions defense walked away with four sacks, but I think that tally is misleading. The first sack, courtesy of DJ Wonnum and a few assists, was a legitimate pass rush win from the defensive line. The second sack was a key third-down sack from safety Chuck Clark. The third and fourth sacks came on back-to-back plays late in the game, one via a Trevor Nowaske spy and one via a seven-man blitz.

Individually, these are great plays, but it masks the problem for the pass rush: consistency. Consistency was an issue even with Hutchinson in the lineup, but you could at least count on him to generate a half dozen pressures per game—he is too good to stop for an entire game. Without Hutchinson, the Lions are going to have to scheme up their pass rush wins more than rely on individual effort.

I think Sheppard did a great job guiding a Hutchinson-less defense on Sunday. The Lions had timely blitzes. The run defense was solid for all but one drive. The secondary once again eliminated the big plays. The team looks far more cohesive and disciplined than when they started.

However, I am still a bit concerned about the pass rush. Outside of those schemed plays, the Lions were not generating much pressure. The Buccaneers' final drive of the first half exemplified that—Mayfield had too much time and delivered perfect passes despite tight coverage. Against better offenses, slow developing pressure is not enough. The Lions have guys with motor, certainly, but they need someone to consistently collapse the pocket without having to dial up a blitz or a stunt. Wonnum is steady and Derrick Moore is progressing (who added another sack to his resume), but the lack of Hutchinson is quite evident—I would like to see more one-on-one wins.

I am really impressed with Williams' growth this season. The deep ball remains his greatest strength, but he makes the most of every down. He is beginning to thrive on the intermediate routes as well, using his speed to bait defenders into covering deep. His hands have improved of late, and he has now has back-to-back games with toe-tap catches along the sideline. Coupled with his stout blocking for a receiver (especially one as skinny as him), there is a lot to love about how Jamo is playing right now.

LaPorta needed a game like this. Given how well the offense had been playing over the last month, they have not needed LaPorta to carry the offense—a few catches a game and some key blocks were more than enough for what Detroit needed. However, it was important for LaPorta to show that he can still be impactful in the receiving game, not only for his own confidence but as a reminder to the world that he is still a top-five tight end in the league.

LaPorta finished with three catches for 62 yards, the biggest of which was his 47-yarder early in the game. This was his most receiving yards in a game since Week 5 versus the Arizona Cardinals. He also sealed the way for Jahmyr Gibbs' second touchdown run of the game.

Last week, I thought that Barnes quietly had one of his best games of the year. This week, I think he quietly had one of his worst games of the year. Tackling was the biggest issue for Barnes, who struggled on multiple occasions to wrap up the ball carrier. The athleticism that shined last week was absent against Tampa Bay. Barnes has the potential to be a sideline-to-sideline type of linebacker that can also bring pressure, but both of those facets were lackluster. Too often he looked out of place. During the times he was in the right spot, a bad angle or tackling attempt gave Tampa Bay more yards.

Considering that the Lions are getting good linebacker play out of their other linebackers, it might be time to dial back Barnes' role on defense.

Clark earned the captaincy for his presence in the locker room, but has also earned it for his play on the field. Clark was a menace versus the Buccaneers, his first game donning the green dot (a role usually reserved for linebackers). He recorded a sack on a perfectly timed blitz in the second quarter. Shortly after, he blew up a Buccaneers receiver to force an incompletion. His tackling was steady too, as he was one of the few players able to wrap up Bucky Irving. On the day, he finished with eight tackles, a sack, a tackle for loss, and a pass defended—this diverse stat line shows how active Clark was across the field.

With Kerby Joseph back in the mix, Brian Branch capable of playing all over, and Clark playing at a high level, the Lions' best defensive look going forward surely has all three safeties on the field.

Winner: K.J. Britt, LBBritt had two impact plays early in the game: he notched a key fourth-down stop, then followed it up with a big special teams tackle. His role continues to grow and he could be a starter before long.

Winner: Malcolm Rodriguez, LBRodriguez continues to be the Lions' best cover linebacker. The Buccaneers' tight ends accomplished very little thanks to Rodriguez locking them down.

Winner: Trevor Nowaske, LBNowaske is the Lions not-so-secret weapon on defense. His athleticism pops on every play, as shown by his sack of Baker Mayfield in which he spied the quarterback like a heat-seeking missile.

Loser: Juice Scruggs, CIt was far from a bad day for Scruggs, but he was struggling versus Vita Vea. Power isn't Scruggs' A-game, so whenever the Lions were running into Vea, they were met with a brick wall. In the future, the Lions need to scheme up help for Scruggs versus big nose tackles like Vea.

Winner: Brock Wright, TEAnother good game from Wright as a blocker, but he was surprisingly active as a receiver, catching two passes for 42 yards (more yards than Amon-Ra St. Brown). This was a good reminder that he can be a sneakily effective pass catcher.

Loser: Isaac TeSlaa, WRTeSlaa had three targets but failed to corral any of them. Two of them were difficult but catchable, especially for the guy known for acrobatic grabs.

Winners: Rock Ya-Sin and Roger McCreary, CBsAnother week where the opposing receivers accomplished very little. Ya-Sin and McCreary have been solid over the past month. Both were officially credited with allowing touchdowns, but Ya-Sin's was a perfect pass from Mayfield and McCreary's was a garbage-time score (and even then, it was another nice outside shoulder throw for Mayfield).

Winner: Kerby Joseph, SIt was modest outing for Joseph, but simply getting him back on the field is a win.

#2743. Prediction markets outlook for stocks in 2026 dims amid AI sell-off

As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off, prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year.

On platform Kalshi, speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. On Oct. 13, those odds were as high as 72%.

Contracts ask traders if the S&P 500 will go above various levels in 2026, and they're resolved using data from S&P Dow Jones Indices.

On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year as investors continued to dump tech stocks, primarily those with exposure to the artificial intelligence build-out. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory, too.

The S&P 500 has slashed its year-to-date gain to just over 2%.

The Stock Trader's Almanac in a Thursday note broadly agreed that the hopes for a December rally are fading, with the caveat that a "Santa rally" could still appear at the end of the year.

"The market is under pressure and more downside can't be ruled out," the note said.

The Stock Trader's Almanac sees 2026 following the year-end pattern of 2018, when the Federal Reserve was in a tightening cycle in a midterm year. The Fed is widely expected to hike rates at its December meeting.

In that scenario, the Stock Trader's Almanac thinks more churn is to come. "The low is more likely in mid- to late December than this week."

#2741. Knicks Bulletin: ‘I like the city of Portland’

If you are like me, you thought you could go to bed early yesterday.

If you are like me, then you realize you were not doing so, because at the end of the day it's the Knicks and they do (yes, after the championship too) Knicks things.

Oh, well, good for all, we stayed awake, and tears rained at the end of the day.

On Mikal Bridges maintaining his composure through a tough start to the season:

"He's the same. Whether he's quote-unquote struggling, he just keeps playing and he doesn't let anything impact him. He's gonna let it fly, and if he can push it, he's gonna push it. He's gonna try to defend, but he's not gonna get too high. He's not gonna get too low, and he's been there and done that. So for him to have the ball in his hands at that point in the game, there's a lot of confidence not only coming from him, but from his teammates and the staff."

On managing the rotation without Karl-Anthony Towns and OG Anunoby:

"I have an idea. I always try to go into the game with a game plan with my minutes sheet. Very seldom do I follow it. We'll have a minutes sheet going into the game."

On Landry Shamet's effort, shooting and defensive versatility:

"I felt he was a really good basketball player coming in. The biggest thing is he plays hard. So even when he's not shooting — because he hasn't shot the ball great every single game — but when he's not shooting the ball, you still feel his impact.

"He plays so hard. He's probably asked to come out of games more than anybody else because he really gasses himself being out there. Every play is that meaningful to him.

"Obviously, you can't leave him open. He's been knocking down shots for the most part. We put him on the ball in pick-and-roll situations, guarding pick-and-roll guys; we put him off the ball so he's had to chase guys. We've even put him on bigger wings and he's done a heck of a job fighting those wings. He's been phenomenal for us. We hope he continues to be that way."

On Shamet exceeding his expectations and being capable of starting for winning teams:

"It's a good question. I didn't know if he'd be this], because I think he can start for a lot of teams in this league, and I'm talking winning teams, not just any old team, but for winning teams.

"I didn't necessarily look at him that way, but I did feel he was definitely a rotational player for this team, because again, you can't teach some of the things that he does out on the floor. They're special. And it's hard to teach that, but in the same breath, you need it in order to have some success, in my opinion."

On James Wiseman's performance against Portland:

"I thought James was great. He ran the floor in both directions, he talked defensively, he impacted the ball at the rim in a phenomenal way. I thought he was really good in his minutes."

On the importance of quick decisions and purposeful movement in the Knicks' offense:

"We have to make sure that every time we cut, it's a scoring cut and our decisions are quick."

On Shamet's off-ball movement creating opportunities for teammates:

"You can tell when a guy goes from Point A to Point B with a little bit of velocity. A guy like Landry Shamet, he is doing it every single time. With him shooting the ball the way he's shooting it, that gravity that he carries when he moves, you can't really see it or feel it if you don't know the game well. But when he moves that quickly from Point A to Point B, everybody is just leaning just a little bit in that direction, which may create an opening or an advantage for your teammate that's away from him."

On getting every Knicks player to move aggressively without the ball:

"Trying to get everybody to do that all the time is huge. Because the defense doesn't have a chance to catch up, they don't have a chance to get set, and they just gotta react. On intentionally pairing Jose Alvarado with Jalen Brunson:

On allowing players' families to travel with the team to build trust:

"In order to get players' trust and get true connectivity, it's anybody associated with them. That's why it's important to have families around."

On Mikal Bridges overcoming his shooting struggles through consistent work:

"Yeah, that's just who he is. #2740. Nets projected to take UConn C Na'jai Hines in 2027 NBA Draft

The Brooklyn Nets (3-12) are still trying to turn their season around after getting off to a less-than-ideal start for a team that was hoping to play better than what the NBA space expected from them. Brooklyn has been trying to improve the chemistry of the team while incorporating multiple new players in the rotation, but there could an interesting player for them to bring in for next season.

"On a per-minute basis, no player in the country combined better shot-blocking and offensive rebounding rates than Na'jai Hines last season," Jonathan Wasserman wrote for Bleacher Report. Wasserman has the Nets selecting UConn center Na'jai Hines with the No. 18 overall pick in the 2027 NBA Draft that the team would be receiving from the New York Knicks due to the Mikal Bridges trade.

"Despite lacking any real creation or scoring skills beyond finishing and post-ups, his paint presence and defense are strong enough for scouts to look past the limited offensive versatility," Wasserman continued on Hines. "He appeared to be in good shape and lighter on his feet during Connecticut's preseason, which could lead to more transition and easy baskets."

Hines, who is in the midst of his sophomore year after spending his freshman season at Seton Hall, is averaging 11.8 points, 6.8 rebounds, and 1.6 blocks per game while shooting 69.0% from the field and 82.6% from the free-throw line. Hines is a big-body center who does all of the damage inside the paint thanks to his size, strength, and ability to protect the rim against dribble penetration.

As of right now, the Nets have Day'Ron Sharpe and Mo Wagner as their centers, but both players have options for next season so if one of them are not on the team next year, Hines could fill that void. There is still plenty of team for general manager Sean Marks and the front office to evaluate the players that would like to add to the team for next season, but Hines could be a guy that fills a potential need for them.

#2738. How Daniel Jones is expected to approach looming free agency with plenty of interest expected

Daniel Jones will wait until it feels just right.

Jones, who is out just six months into the $88 million deal he signed before the season, is expected to draw much interest, possibly from the Patriots, Cardinals and Ravens, among others.

However, sources are saying he will wait and could likely help come the playoffs if a team is navigating an injury.

Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones (17) looks on from the sideline during a game against the Houston Texans in Houston, Texas, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

#2737. ‘You just offended most, if not all, of Mexico’: Nick Bosa faces criticism after ‘condescending’ comments about Mexican fans

The San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings will meet in Mexico City on Sunday Night Football in a game that could go a long way toward deciding the NFC's No. 1 seed. But ahead of the big matchup, 49ers superstar defensive end Nick Bosa managed to make headlines for all the wrong reasons.

Bosa drew backlash this week when he suggested that fans in Mexico City need to be told when to cheer during the game. Now, longtime 49ers reporter Grant Cohn has offered Bosa some "friendly advice," saying that his comments came across as "condescending" to the host country.

During a press conference this week, Bosa was asked about the atmosphere when the 49ers last played in Mexico City in 2022. He remembered the crowd being loud, but he had a request for the fans this time around.

"Yeah, I kind of want … I think we need some information given to the fans so they know when to cheer," Bosa said, via NBC Sports Bay Area. "Because they just chant the whole time. If we can kind of teach them, no offense to them and their soccer cheering techniques, but if they can cheer when we're on defense, that would be great."

Needless to say, those comments didn't go over well with a lot of people, including plenty of reporters who cover the NFL. Several members of the media were quick to call Bosa out, including Cohn, who said he "was not expecting Nick Bosa to offend the entire country of Mexico before the 49ers even arrive."

On Saturday, Cohn followed up with a two-minute video offering Bosa some advice. He opened by suggesting that Bosa probably didn't mean to offend anyone.

"Nicholas, Nicholas, Nicholas, you've done it again," Cohn said. "You're a man of few words, but when you do talk, you often get yourself in trouble. And I feel like sometimes you're just misunderstood, like this time. Like, now, you just offended most, if not all, of Mexico. The entire country. And I don't think you meant to do that."

Cohn acknowledged that Bosa was likely "just talking ball," but he made it clear that the comments still came off the wrong way.

"But see, it comes across as condescending," Cohn said. "Because they know. They watch football. They know exactly how Americans cheer; they just don't cheer like that because they want to cheer their way. Frankly, it's a lot more fun."

Cohn then offered Bosa a simple rule to follow in the future to avoid these sorts of situations.

"In the future, Nicholas, anytime you're invited somewhere and you're a guest, it's bad form to tell the host what to do. In any walk of life. You're the guest. What you say is, 'It's so nice to be here. Thank you to the entire country of Mexico for being so generous and welcoming. Can't wait to play at Stadium Azteca.' That's all you say. Period!" Cohn said.

"Just like if you were to go to someone's house for dinner. You'd say, 'Hey, man, thank you for dinner and thank you having me.' Not like, 'Yo, turn the heater up to 78 and give me eight ice cubes in my drink. And make it a half-Coke, half-orange soda mixture right now. Actually, I want peanut butter and jelly.' That's what you don't do!" he added.

Clearly, Bosa will have plenty of motivation to get that first sack of the season on Sunday night. It will be interesting to see how the crowd in Mexico City treats him when he does.

#2736. Inside the Suns: Ryan Dunn, Koa Peat, a wake up call?

Welcome to Inside the Suns, a deep down analysis of the current Phoenix Suns team in which the Fantable — a round table of Bright Siders — give their takes on the Suns' latest issues and news.

GuarGuar: I've been really impressed with Ryan so far this season. He's showing more control and poise in his game. He's not recklessly driving at 100 mph to the rim every time he touches the ball. The jump shot mechanics look better, and he's been impressive as a roll man this year. He's been a pleasant surprise.

zenzino: I love it! How could I not? As I wrote in a previous Fantable (or thread, I can't remember), Dunn was considered by many (including me) to be the odd man out for rotational minutes this season. However, he became the poster child for the fact that progress is not linear. After a sophomore year where the improvement was slight (especially alongside Oso's improvement), Dunn has made a leap in his third year.

We never questioned his defense. He reportedly put in a lot of work on his shot this off-season. As he said himself, he 'has to trust in the work'. This becomes evident during a game. When he has time to think about it, he'll either pass up a shot or look more like last year's shooting. When he doesn't have time to think, his shot looks really good and goes in more often than not.

The more he works, and the less time he has to think, the shots will go down, and he'll gain enough confidence to think and shoot.

This is also a lesson not to give up on Sheer. He may have a sophomore slump this season, but that doesn't mean he's not working and could come out later in the season or his third year to make a Dunn-like leap.

Ashton: I am a little curious why Dunn's minutes seem to vary by game. He is clearly the next man up at the power forward position. But, thus far, I have not paid enough attention to Dunn on the Fantable and he is impressing me as a future breakout candidate to start. So, my bad on not giving Ryan Dunn more love early.

Also, Brooks said he would be willing to play bench minutes? Jaw hits the floor as he is coming off one of his best games against the Sacramento Kings. He stated that is to work on his playmaking with the better spacing that the bench provides. I applaud his heroic statement, but I am calling BS. The real reason is so he can terrorize opposing bench unit defenses into therapy with his constant chirping. Still, an intriguing thought to consider. Does Ott buy-in? I doubt it.

That would make Ryan Dunn the starter for minutes if that were to come true. Some of the Suns' lineups would be rife for consideration in the comment sections.

OldAz: Personally, I love what Ryan has done this year. He has taken advantage of the lowered expectations, especially compared to last season when he was expected to come in and capture a larger role only to struggle with the new system and get stuck behind a number of veteran guards.

This season, most had written him off coming into the season and were fine throwing him into whatever trade would accomplish moving whatever core player that fan wanted to move. Instead, he ratcheted up his defensive intensity and the speed at which he plays and has made a significant impact.  My only complaint is with the coaching staff that seems to have way too long of a leash for veteran players to play emotionless, effortless basketball and only give a player like Ryan a few minutes despite their obvious positive impact on the overall result on the floor.

Ryan is not going to fill up the stat sheet, but he is going to hustle on defense, compete for rebounds, and is willing to shoot or drive when he is left open.  He is a perfect complement to Booker or any of the other "star" players on the court when Ott chooses to play him.  He is one of those players (along with Goodwin, Gillespie, and Kennard) that you can pair with either center and 2 of the core starters and get a pretty decent lineup because of their hustle and energy. The only difference is he is the only one of those 4 that also brings some length to the court.

I'm not overly worried about the recent little injuries, as I believe he has figured out that his energy and effort mean more than the stats he puts up each night. Hopefully Ott is starting to figure out the same thing.

Rod: I hated to see him get hurt in the Jazz game. Hopefully. he won't be out long because he's become an important part of the Suns' rotation. His offensive impact hasn't been great, but he's been playing more under control on that end and making positive contributions, both inside (5th most dunks on the team in just the 10th most minutes per game) and outside (42.3% from three). His biggest areas of impact have been on defense and in rebounding (per 36, he's tied with Bridges for 2nd at 8.6).

I'll admit that I was one of the people who was almost ready to give up on Ryan this season if he didn't show some improvement. Happily, he's come through for us and is playing very well and under control.

GuarGuar: I really hope it was a wake-up call. This starting lineup has been awful together, and the metrics don't lie. The Jalen Green PG experiment has been an abject failure, and the sooner we move off of it, the better we will be. zenzino: I guess? How many wake-up calls do they need?

It occurred to me the other day that it is the fans' job to (over)react from game to game and the coaches/FO's job NOT to react from game to game.

Ashton: I hate this question. Beat LA, Beat LA!

Which is exactly what the Suns need: beating the teams they are supposed to beat, but picking up a few wins against the teams that are not (Houston and Denver). The Lakers were not on the bingo card in the W category.

Still, Ott probably wisely threw in the towel against a very good Lakers squad and allowed his starters to watch real basketball from the sidelines without getting injured. I was fine with it from a strategic point of view, but I am not fine with it from a fan point of view.

OldAz: Maybe. It certainly couldn't have hurt as we have seen a better version of Brooks and Green since then, with more focus on the defensive end and moving the ball on offense instead of always forcing their own shots. I think Booker and Bridges were already playing well, but it really requires all the starters to be on the same page for that group to succeed.  The better play and effort from all has also allowed Ott to play a little more randomly with lineups.

Now the question is if the recent successes are more about this improved play and more diverse lineup combinations, or just a product of playing lesser teams that the Suns should handle like the Kings and Jazz.

Rod: You could call it that, or you could call it a message from Ott, "Play with some heart or you'll sit and watch your teammates show you what that means." Whatever you want to call it, it seems to have worked in the games since then.

You can have all the talent in the world, but without effort, players are just wasting the fans' time (and patience) when they're just going through the motions. GuarGuar: Koa is probably only useful as a small-ball 5 right now until he develops a jump shot, which looks to be a ways away. zenzino: I think it's pretty telling that he has spent zero time with the Valley Suns. My wild speculation is that Ott wants him with the team and ready to play.

His true shooting is 68.2 percent and his usage is 21.1. The plus-minus is 3.8. These numbers come from very few minutes, so they say little yet. His minutes have ranged from 1.3 to 8.2 in a night, and he has not scored in three of the eight games.

#2734. Despite off day, Bills too much to handle for Dolphins in Week 11

In the immediate aftermath of the Buffalo Bills' Week 11 win over the Miami Dolphins, many will scratch their heads wondering what they watched unfold Sunday afternoon. To be clear her: What a strange win by the Bills. Buffalo's offense barely resembled the group most have watched in 2026.

It's important to step back a moment, however, and realize that Buffalo has built a good, often great team. The Bills haven't trailed in a game since October 18 against the Las Vegas Raiders (hat tip: Carson Hayek). Buffalo has also three consecutive games by 17 or more points. What about the defense? Well, that group hasn't allowed a touchdown in three straight games.

It may be true that the Bills didn't execute their most impressive game plan of the season, and that they strayed too far away from their true identity until crunch time. It's clear that quarterback Josh Allen didn't have his typically dominant effort against the Dolphins, even though he did throw for 304 yards, but he didn't need to play lights out.

Interestingly, Allen attempted zero rushes. In fact, during a first-half 4th & 1 situation, Allen handed the ball off to running back James Cook III, who scampered through the right side of the line to move the chains. The intent seemed clear that the move was to avoid exposing Allen to unnecessary contact, at least. That move can only work so well when you ask the quarterback to drop back 45 times. As a result, Miami's defense hit Allen six times, sacking him on three occasions.

Most believed that Buffalo would use their dominant rushing attack to try and wear down the Dolphins' trio of backup defensive tackles in the first half. It was tough sledding early, perhaps surprisingly to Brady and the offense, and Cook had just 13 carries for 36 yards and a touchdown at halftime. Allen was forced into two consecutive interceptions late in the second quarter, with a third erased due to penalty.

Then consider the decisions on special teams. First there was the surprising fake punt that proved successful thanks to a pretty 30-yard throw and completion by rookie punter Tommy Doman Jr. Doubling down on surprise (as much as is possible in today's rulebook), the Bills then decided to declare an onside kick attempt after a score. Analyst Adam Archuleta wondered if they saw something on film to warrant the try, and if they'd take the delay-of-game penalty instead of running it. We know now, they didn't attempt the onside try.

As has been the case in so many games this season, the second half was a different story on offense. The return to form just took a bit longer. Late in the fourth quarter, Archuleta mentioned the curious shift in game plan on offense. Understandably, they had entered four-minute offense territory, but the point was well-understood as a discourse on their pass-heavy approach early in action.

The Bills looked like the better team all game long, but it also seemed like they missed out on a lot of points they'd otherwise score. They don't call the NFL a week-to-week league for nothing, and divisional games are always tough to predict regardless of record and any familiarity (or lack thereof) with the opponent.

I keep being called back to the strangeness of this game. Is it possible they were using Week 11 as an opportunity to put a fair amount of new things/alternate tendencies on tape for the gauntlet facing them the next month? Certainly, there's potential for it to be the case.

It's true that Buffalo has a very short week to prepare for the 8-2 Kansas City Chiefs, which could have played into the offensive game plan when you consider Allen's shift to playing dropback, quick-release football from the pocket — that also erased him from the rushing column.

I'm not the only one to consider this move, as evidenced by a tweet from ESPN Bills beat reporter Nick Suss that wondered if they were "giving the Chiefs a crapton of looks they have to prepare for on a short week, even if the Bills don't plan on using any of them again on Thursday."

Is it possible that situation played into the decisions made in Week 11? Again, One Bills Drive will never admit to it, and rightfully so, but it's possible that they used today's game as an opportunity to stress KC's pre-game load ahead of Thursday night.

True or otherwise, it's difficult to spend too much time ripping apart a team that blows out its opponent, while covering the enormous 16.5-point spread. The Bills continue looking really good even on off days, and Buffalo once again prove to be too much to handle for the Dolphins. You could say that about most of their opponents right now.

Will that the case Thursday? We'll find out if the Bills can add to the right kind of "just deserts" for your Thanksgiving Day celebration!

#2733. The Nasdaq is in freefall. Here's one stock to look at

I asked Claude after Friday's close what I should do about the tanking stock market. Its advice was surprisingly useful: avoid panic selling and look for opportunities. A 40 VIX, which it touched Friday, might provide those opportunities. Specifically, a higher VIX (higher options premiums) signals fear, but it also creates an opportunity to sell elevated premium in some premium stocks, like Amazon.

Amazon's cloud business is growing at its fastest pace in nearly five years. AWS revenue rose 39.3% YoY in the third quarter, and management reported a $578 billion backlog. Trailing 12-month operating cash flow rose 29% to $168.3 billion. However, infrastructure investment accelerated, resulting in more than $42 billion in negative cash flow. The competing forces of accelerating growth and the cost of supplying it could keep the stock in its range over the next four weeks. Its shares are only off 14% from its recent highs, comparatively better than the Nasdaq Composite's near 19% decline.

AWS demand supports the lower end of the range. The backlog gives Amazon a basis for adding capacity even as investors scrutinize the cash cost. Cash spending could temper an upside rerating.

The next leg higher may require evidence that new capacity can earn attractive returns at this scale, and that evidence may be in short supply over the next couple of months.

Max risk — Unlimited on the uncovered call, but one should think of the trade as risking getting short at a net price above $290, a nearly 13% premium to today's closing price. The downside loss would reach $22,910 per strangle if AMZN fell to zero. The credit is roughly 2.3% of a $260 reference share price over four weeks, or nearly 30% on a simple annualized basis. That comparison uses the share price as its denominator. Actual return on capital depends on margin and the cost to close or settle the trade.

Buying in bear markets, as the Nasdaq just touched, is never easy. But those opportunities don't present themselves too often. What are you going to do with it?

#2730. Joe Mazzulla downplays disastrous third straight loss: ‘We played well enough’

For the third straight time, the Boston Celtics went out like a dud, collapsing against the two-win Sacramento Kings on Saturday night without Jayson Tatum, Derrick White and Mitchell Robinson. But head coach Joe Mazzulla was rather dismissive afterward.

"I think we played well enough to win the game," Mazzulla told reporters, per CLNS Media, after Boston's 97-96, "and they made more shots than we did, and made a couple of more plays down the stretch. You take a look at the process of the game, we played well and lost. So that's what you take from [it] and move on to tomorrow."

Mazzulla turned to Paul George and Payton Pritchard to lead the pack. They shared the floor with Sam Hauser, Hugo González and Neemias Queta in Boston's starting lineup. Yet the team's strongest and most efficient contribution didn't come from any of them. It came from 39-year-old guard Mike Conley, who had made just four appearances for Boston entering the night, averaging eight minutes per game before receiving 18 minutes off the bench in Sacramento.

Conley scored 19 points, converting his first six consecutive shot attempts, while adding four rebounds, three assists and two steals. From the looks of it, Conley had himself a heroic, game-saving performance in the works, good enough to get the Celtics back in the column. He was active, up to speed and turned back the clock to his vintage Memphis Grizzlies days, even though he sat on the bench for the entire first and third quarters.

Nov 21, 2026; Sacramento, California, USA; Boston Celtics forward Paul George (13) reacts during the third quarter against the Sacramento Kings at Golden 1 Center. Mandatory Credit: Justine Willard-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Had it not been for Conley's out-of-the-blue scoring outburst, the Kings might've run the Celtics out of the building.

"He kept us in it," Mazzulla said. "Tried to finish the game with him as much as we could. Thought he was great on both ends of the floor and tonight's the reason why you have a guy like that on your roster, and he gave us a chance to win tonight."

Conley stood tall as Boston's lone bright spot, tying George for the team's lead in scoring while finishing as Boston's plus-minus leader (+17).

The Celtics performed well below their standard, underscoring the impact Tatum's absence had against a Kings team that leads the Western Conference in turnovers (17.5), boasts the NBA's second-lowest-scoring offense (106.8 points) and had won just one of its first 15 games entering Saturday night.

Without their superstar, the wheels fell off the wagon.

In the third quarter, Mazzulla's group got outscored 35-13 and went 0-for-13 from three.

With back-to-back rest days, the underperformance was all the more inexcusable.

Boston finished the night shooting 33.7 percent from the field, going 34-for-101. They shot 22.4 percent from 3-point range, going 13-for-58 and setting a franchise record for most misses (45) in a single game. At the free-throw line, they went 15-for-25, adding further fuel to the fire.

George went 6-for-21, Pritchard went 4-for-17 and Baylor Scheierman shot 2-for-11.

Coming off consecutive losses to the Orlando Magic and Denver Nuggets, this was their ugliest dud by far.

In the fourth quarter, the Celtics traded baskets with Sacramento as the clock ticked down. Queta hit a go-ahead 3-pointer from the corner with 3:47 remaining, only for Kings rookie Darius Acuff Jr. to drain the equalizer, also from beyond the arc. George grabbed an offensive rebound and finished the putback layup with 49 seconds left. Acuff answered by drawing a foul and sinking both free throws at the other end. Pritchard sank a clutch fadeaway jumper to give Boston a 96-95 lead with 12 seconds remaining. Then the Celtics failed to protect the glass on the ensuing possession.

Acuff challenged González off the inbound, drove past him and missed his right-handed layup. But Sacramento's Keegan Murray leaped over Devin Carter to secure the offensive rebound and finish the putback, giving the Kings a 97-96 lead and leaving Boston with just five seconds for redemption.

For the game, Pritchard was handed the ball against Murray but failed to create enough space for a clean look, capping an already miserable performance with a wasted opportunity.

Pritchard finished with nine points and missed all eight of his 3-point attempts, which he owned up to.

"It's frustrating," Pritchard told reporters. "I just got to play better. I gotta do more, so a lot of that is on me in the third quarter and stuff like that. So it's my fault for that one."

Pritchard on the final possession: "Obviously didn't get to a good enough spot, and [Murray] played good defense. But probably need to try to find a better look, though."

The Celtics have lost three consecutive regular-season games for the first time since opening last season with three straight defeats. They suffered their most humbling loss yet, deservedly getting served their lunch by arguably the worst team in the NBA.

"I thought we competed at a high level through just a drought offensively where we couldn't make shots," Mazzulla said. "And again, you have to stick to the process of it. I thought we played well enough to win, and we just didn't. They made a few more plays than we did."

Winning and playing "well enough" to win aren't mutually exclusive. However, the Celtics didn't meet the threshold necessary to leave Sacramento victorious. Their result was entirely warranted.

#2729. Top Wall Street analysts favor these 3 dividend stocks for strong returns

Investors often favor dividend stocks for their regular income and the promise of potential share price appreciation. But selecting the right dividend stocks from a huge pool of companies can be difficult.

Top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend-paying stocks, as their recommendations are backed by thorough analysis of a company's financials.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Devon Energy (DVN), an independent oil and natural gas exploration and production company, reported better-than-expected third-quarter results. The company announced a quarterly dividend of 32 cents per share for the fourth quarter, payable December 30. Based on the fixed dividends paid over the trailing 12 months, DVN yields 2.85%.

After hosting a virtual investor meeting with management, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Devon, with a price target of $59. Mehta said that he is now more confident in management's outlook for delivering strong near-term capital returns as well as efforts to drive operational efficiencies and productivity gains.

Devon sees an opportunity to increase share repurchases, driven by solid free cash flow (FCF), contributions from the Eagle Ford divestiture and continued improvement in the balance sheet, Mehta said. Devon expects share buybacks worth more than $1 billion in Q4 2026, up from $414 million in the third quarter, backed by a strong pricing backdrop and improved capital efficiency.

Mehta, a 5-star analyst, said Devon expects about $6.3 billion of excess FCF in 2027, including about $3.5 billion of net proceeds from the Eagle Ford sale. That would enable the company to accelerate buybacks while progressing toward its goal of reducing gross debt to about $9 billion by early 2027. Mehta noted that under DVN's framework to return up to 70% of annual FCF, management favors share buybacks as it believes the stock is discounted compared to large-cap peers.

"Management expects continued capital efficiency gains from merger synergies, extended laterals, surfactant adoption and development of the newly acquired federal acreage," Mehta said.

Energy Transfer (ET), is a limited partnership that operates about 140,000 miles of pipeline and associated energy infrastructure. The company recently announced third-quarter results showing net income per common unit growing about 18% year-over-year, to 33 cents. ET's cash distribution for Q3 2026 was 34.25 cents per common unit, up more than 3% year-over-year. At an annualized distribution of $1.37 per share, Energy Transfer yields more than 7%.

TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Energy Transfer with a price target of $25. The company delivered better-than-expected Q3 results and announced the 1.2 billion cubic feet per day (bcf/d) South Mississippi Pipeline, a 215-mile, 36-inch natural gas line linking the Perryville Hub to the Florida Gas Transmission (FGT) network, Gabelman said. Gabelman also highlighted management's commentary about optimization initiatives contributing an incremental $800 million to 2026 earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, a larger benefit than in recent years. "A return to less commodity volatility should the [Middle East] war end could bring some relative downside, though this is offset by continued strong growth prospects," he said.

Earnings were driven by solid price realizations, partially offset by higher depletion, depreciation and amortization and purchased commodities.

Margolin also noted COP's dividend increase and said the accelerated buyback enabled by current commodity prices could further support long-term dividend growth. #2728. Fantasy Football Week 11 RB Report: Another fumble makes D'Andre Swift tough to trust, plus more backfield splits

Let's take a second to appreciate the backup running back and the importance of having that insurance on your bench. Emmett Johnson drew another start in place of the injured Kenneth Walker III on Sunday. For the third time in four weeks, the rookie back went for 22+ fantasy points on a hefty 23 carries for 105 yards and a score, plus four catches for 38 yards. Most of that damage was done well before the game clock wound down in the fourth quarter.

If you're a Walker manager who was smart enough to add Johnson back after Week 8, nice work. If you were like me (in one league) and didn't grab Johnson to replace Walker, well … it's been a rough watch the past month or so.

In this piece, we talk a lot about backfield splits and depth running backs, specifically, in an attempt to inform you for future weeks. Let's see what the highlights and box scores show us that we can use for fantasy football going into Week 12 and the Thanksgiving week slate.

It was an ugly week in general for the Bears offense in a spot we thought could produce points, considering the team had an implied total around 30. Instead, we got inconsistency, particularly in the run game despite the return of Kyle Monangai. He had missed the past five games due to turf toe and a thumb injury. This was also an elite matchup for running backs; New Orleans entered Week 11 allowing the sixth-most rushing yards per game and sixth-most rushing TDs this season.

While Swift got to an OK floor for fantasy purposes because of a short TD catch, he could be back in the doghouse after another lost fumble, his third of the season. As a result, we saw carries for fourth-string RB Salvon Ahmed, with Roschon Johnson leaving the game early due to an ankle injury. Monangai also wasn't his usual efficient self, though we're willing to give him a pass coming back after a long absence.

Let's talk about Swift first. In games following a Swift fumble, Swift maintained a heavy workload with 22 touches in Week 3 and 13 in Week 5 (no Caleb Williams). So Swift shouldn't lose his role, but he also hasn't been all that impressive. He doesn't have a carry longer than 15 yards since Week 1 and doesn't have a catch that went for more than 13 yards since Week 2. Ben Johnson could opt to lean more on Monangai, but he and Swift have had a relatively even split of the carries when both are healthy, with Swift being more of a threat in the passing game. Ahmed also didn't look all that bad and could leech a few touches.

The next two weeks aren't ideal, either. The Bears get the Lions on Thanksgiving on the road and the Jaguars in Week 13, two of the worst matchups for RBs in fantasy. It will be tough to count on both Swift and Monangai as anything more than flex options in the short term, and after that we could see the latter take on more work if he can stay healthy. The matchups soften a bit in a key stretch from Weeks 14-16.

Maybe it was the Panthers defense but the Ravens offense looks revived with Jacoby Brissett under center. At least for fantasy purposes. Baltimore scored 33 points and had over 400 yards of offense Sunday in the narrow loss to Carolina. For real life, it was brutal. For fantasy managers, it was a sigh of relief for those with Henry and Zay Flowers.

But we're here to talk about the backfield specifically, where Henry got back to work with his highest total on the ground since Week 5, when he went for over 100 yards rushing. He now has four total TDs in the past three games and a useful nine catches in the past two. A lost fumble put a minor dent in his final total as well.

Despite getting back on track the past two weeks, at least from a fantasy points perspective, there's still cause for concern for Henry managers. And it's in the form of Hill.

The backup RB put together another strong outing, nearly reaching 100 total yards on just 10 touches with a 19-yard TD before halftime. Hill also had a 36-yard long rush in the game that resulted in a fumble just before scoring. All in all, he continues to showcase big-play ability. He entered the game averaging 6.8 yards per carry and had 11.5 per against the Panthers. That's going to keep Hill involved.

Looking ahead, how Baltimore performs down the stretch could play a factor in how this backfield looks for fantasy managers. With six straight losses, sitting at 4-7, the Ravens aren't entirely out of the playoff picture. They still have four division games left (two against the Steelers). But a few more losses could sink Baltimore and that could lead to less work for Henry and more for Hill. We recommended Hill in the early waiver piece going into Week 12.

Henry is still an RB2 for fantasy but there's also the Week 13 bye — not ideal. Hill has shown he can be an RB3/flex with upside. If you have Henry, you need Hill on your bench. If you're looking for a potential league-winner late in the season, Hill has that upside if the chips fall right.

Kamara can't keep getting away with this, can he?

Last week, it was a tilting five touches for 14 total yards and two scores. This week, it's just TWO yards on two touches, but another touchdown. Seven other carries went to various skill position players and QB Tyler Shough. But at least it was a decent showing by Etienne in his second game back after being placed on injured reserve after Week 3.

It wasn't a dominant performance by Etienne but it was good enough for his managers to trust him back in their lineups. Most of his 76 yards came on a 46-yard run, but that's fine; we wanted to see Etienne get back to making big plays, and that was his biggest of the 2026 season. The volume was also a great sign with Audric Estimé a healthy scratch for Week 11; the backfield was all Etienne's.

The larger issue is the Saints offense. It's not performing up to par, like the boat races and shootouts we saw in flashes last season after Shough took over. The O-line isn't great and Shough has regressed a bit. The rest of the fantasy schedule lines up well for points (at CIN, vs. GB, at CAR), which is a plus. But we need to see some progress from Kellen Moore's group overall in order to have faith in Etienne as an RB2.

The back has that potential but he'll need 15-20 touches and a few big plays mixed in. Etienne is going to lose snaps to Kamara and New Orleans likes using the vet in the red zone. This game has us putting Etienne back in the RB2/3 range, while Kamara is only a risky, TD-dependent flex.

#2727. Is Raiders TE Brock Bowers Playing vs. Broncos?

The Las Vegas Raiders were prepared for the worst when star tight end Brock Bowers had to leave the Week 10 game against the Seattle Seahawks with an ankle injury. While head coach Klint Kubiak called the injury "significant," Bowers was able to practice this week.

The Raiders listed him as questionable, which was a good sign that he could play in Week 11 against the Denver Broncos. Unfortunately, he wasn't able to get ready in time. The Raiders officially listed him as inactive vs. the Broncos.

This is pretty bad news for the Raiders. Bowers is the only player on offense consistently making plays. Without him, it's hard to see how they'll be able to score points against a very good Broncos defense.

Michael Mayer, Tre Tucker, Jalen Nailor and Jack Bech really have to step up if the Raiders are going to have any chance.

The team now just has to hope that this is a one-week absence for Bowers. He's already missed two games previously. He's an elite player when he's on the field, but the injury issues are starting to pile up. The Raiders' bye week is coming up, so they may choose to rest him until they get through that.

The Raiders were methodical in how they first decided to play rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza, but there could be some regret. His debut was against the No. 1 defense in the NFL, and it didn't go well.

Now he gets to play another elite defense without his best offensive weapon. The Raiders just need to hope that Mendoza can get out of the game unscathed. It's hard to imagine they'll be able to score very many points against the Broncos. They can't run the ball, and the wide receivers have been terrible.

Now, the Broncos' offense also isn't very good. If the Raiders' defense can have a good game, they'll have a chance to pull off the upset, but it's highly unlikely this game ends up being a shootout.

Mendoza only has one game under his belt, but he gained a lot of fans during his time in college. He may have had an underwhelming debut, but expectations are still very high for him.

Broncos defensive coordinator Vance Joseph has a lot of respect for Mendoza's game.

"He's got the great size, great arm talent, he's athletic, he's smart," Joseph said, via Raiders.com. "He was poised, I mean did not look shook at all. The first half [against Seahawks] was really good, I think once [Brock] Bowers went out, it kind of hurt the game plan a little bit, but the first drive – I mean it's 11 plays, touchdown. And he's making plays with his legs. he's making throws. … But he is poised, and he can make every single throw and it's not too big for him."

Mendoza is going to be seeing the Broncos a lot over the course of his career, so he has to hope he's able to make a strong first impression.
